sections.html: Asellus aquaticus, also known as the Water louse, Water shrimp, Water slate or Aquatic sowbug, is a small freshwater crustacean in the family Asellidae. It is related to woodlice. It is very hardy and can live in polluted, acidic or alkaline water, water with low oxygen, and even brackish conditions. Lifespan is about 1 year, up to 1.5 years.

Sometimes used as live food for medium to large bottom-feeding fish. In shrimp breeding tanks, keeping them together is not recommended: not because of aggression but because of food competition, faster reproduction, and tolerance to conditions that kill shrimp.

Asellus aquaticus is one of the most common freshwater crustaceans and is widely distributed throughout Europe and North America. It is associated with a temperate climate and has been recorded from the Mediterranean in the south to Scandinavia in the north.

It is hypothesized that it arrived in Europe around 8 to 12 million years ago through the brackish Paratethys basin.

High densities are found in stagnant or slow-flowing waters with organic pollution, especially near sewage outfalls, but also in relatively clean waters with high levels of natural organic matter. The species is eurybiont and thrives in a wide range of conditions, including slightly brackish surface waters and subterranean freshwater habitats.

It is absent from marine waters and from fast-flowing streams and rivers.
To remove them: remove hiding places, deep clean the filter and vacuum the substrate, increase water flow, reduce excess food and algae, and use traps with a leaf or vegetable placed in the evening.

• Tolerant of poor water quality and organic pollution; tolerates significant salinity.
  • Resilient to low oxygen and high levels of unionized ammonia (about 5 times more resistant to low oxygen and 2 times more to unionized ammonia than Gammarus pulex).
  • pH: 100% survival at 4.5–11.0, optimum 6.5–9.0.
  • Temperature: 5–30°C, most active in cooler months. High temperature reduces growth, survival and reproduction.

Change temperature gradually; abrupt changes of more than 5 degrees can cause temperature shock.

An efficient detritivore with a broad diet: leaf litter, biofilm, microorganisms, fungi, algae and more. The primary food is decaying vegetation; they appear to prefer fungi.

In the aquarium they eat almost everything. To recreate natural conditions, periodically add a few dry leaves; only the veins will remain. Do not add green leaves, which contain much sugar and can increase organic waste. Make sure leaves are clean and untreated.

They are safe in planted tanks: they graze on plants that are already dying.

The water louse crawls slowly along the substrate or decaying plant debris. It is fully aquatic and practically helpless in air. It does not truly swim, but can propel itself through the water with a jerky, hopping motion.

It has two defences: staying motionless, or autotomy (shedding limbs, which later regenerate). In dry seasons it buries itself in mud and enters torpor.

As scavengers they act as a clean-up crew, breaking down organic matter and decaying plants. They do not damage eggs of egg scatterers.

• Males are larger than females.
  • Males' first pair of legs has apophyses, absent in females. The 4th pair is smaller and curved, used to hold the female.
  • Females have oostegites forming a brood pouch on the front underside of the body.

Usually two generations per year (spring and autumn cohorts). Breeding starts in spring when water reaches about 7–8°C. Sexual maturity is reached at 1.5 to 3 months and about 3–4 mm.

The male guards the female by carrying her for 5–7 days until she molts. Fertilization is possible only for about 24 hours after the molt, then the male releases her.

Within 2–10 hours a brood pouch develops and orange eggs are deposited, usually 30–150. Incubation takes 23 to 35 days depending on temperature. Juveniles of about 1 mm are released and are independent.

• Size: typically 5–10 mm, males slightly larger than females; up to 2 cm is an exception.
  • Body: flattened, segmented, elongated, with overlapping plates; brown or gray, sometimes mottled. Cave forms have reduced pigmentation and eyes.
  • Body segments: 5 cephalic, 8 thoracic and 7 abdominal; the last abdominal segment is the telson.
  • Seven pairs of walking legs and a pair of long antennae.

Wild-caught Asellus aquaticus can be intermediate hosts for parasitic worms (acanthocephalosis), but infection of aquarium fish is rare.
